problems.title: Loads per FMA
problems.statement: An r × c thread tile loads r values of A and c of B per k and does r·c FMAs.
problems.solution: 0.5, 0.25 and 0.625. Square tiles minimise loads for a given number of accumulators.

problems.title: FMA fraction with vector loads
problems.statement: 8 × 8 thread tile; per k, the thread loads 8 A values and 8 B values from shared memory as float4s, then does 64 FMAs.
problems.solution: (a) 4. (b) 64/68 = 94.1%: the instruction ceiling is now close to peak, and other limits (latency, occupancy, memory) take over.

problems.title: What the registers cost
problems.statement: An 8 × 8 tile kernel uses 64 accumulators + 16 operands + about 20 for addresses and loop state: 100 registers. 256-thread blocks.
problems.solution: (a) 3328. (b) 19 warps fit, so 2 blocks. (c) 25%. Low, by design.

problems.title: Is low occupancy enough?
problems.statement: Same kernel: 16 warps per SM (4 per scheduler). Each warp has 64 independent FMAs per k step; FMA latency is 4 cycles.

parts.prompt: Independent FMAs a scheduler can choose from per k step?
Can the scheduler issue an FMA every cycle?
options: Yes: far more independent work than the 4-cycle latency needs
No: it needs 16 warps per scheduler

hints: To issue every cycle with latency 4 you need 4 independent instructions in flight.
problems.solution: 256 independent FMAs available against 4 needed: occupancy is irrelevant here, ILP covers it. That's Volkov's point in its purest form.

problems.title: Tiles versus parallelism
problems.statement: 64 × 64 block tiles on the GW-1 (16 SMs).

parts.prompt: Fraction of SMs busy for 128 × 128, in %?

problems.solution: 16 blocks fill the GW-1 once; 4 blocks leave 75% idle. Small GEMMs need smaller tiles, split-K, or Stream-K (Part 5's paper).

problems.title: The biggest square thread tile
problems.statement: A thread may use 128 registers; about 24 go to addresses and loop state. An t × t tile needs $t^2$ accumulators and $2t$ operand registers.
problems.solution: t = 9 gives 99 ≤ 104; t = 10 gives 120. Powers of two keep indexing and vector loads simple, so 8 × 8 is the standard choice.

problems.title: Shared memory for a block tile

parts.prompt: Bytes for one stage of A and B tiles?

problems.solution: 8 KB per stage, 16 KB double-buffered: modest, because the reuse now happens in registers.

problems.title: Reuse at the block level
problems.statement: Per k-step a block loads (BM + BN)·BK values into shared memory and performs BM·BN·BK FMAs.

parts.prompt: FMAs per value loaded from global memory, for 128 × 128?

problems.solution: 64 and 32. Bigger block tiles raise DRAM-level intensity; bigger thread tiles raise register-level intensity. Both are bounded by on-chip storage.

problems.title: Reading the A tile
problems.statement: In a register-tiled kernel, the 16 threads that share a row of the thread grid all read the same 8 A values at each k.

parts.prompt: Why store A transposed in shared memory?
options: To avoid bank conflicts on the B reads
So each thread's 8 values of one k are contiguous, for a float4 read

problems.solution: (a) Lanes reading the same word get a broadcast. (b) A is row-major in global memory, so a column slice (fixed k) is strided; transposing while staging makes it contiguous for vector loads.

problems.title: The hierarchy
problems.statement: Match each level of a GEMM's tiling to what it buys.

options: Fewer DRAM/L2 accesses (reuse across a block)
Fewer shared-memory loads per FMA (register reuse)
A shape for the warp's shared-memory reads (broadcasts, no conflicts)

hints: Each level raises reuse at the level above it.
problems.solution: Block tiles reduce global traffic, thread tiles reduce shared traffic, and warp tiles arrange the warp's accesses so the shared memory serves them in one pass.
